text.p: Dial "3" for Europe -- at least we will if the European Commission has its way.
In a wide-ranging plan to overhaul the European Union's telephone numbering system, the Commission said it wanted "3" to become the first figure of every international call to Europe.
The plan, outlined in a discussion document published on Wednesday, also says subscribers should keep their numbers when they switch telephone companies.
They should also be able to dial the same toll-free number -- beginning with 388 -- from anywhere in Europe to order goods or call for emergency roadside assistance.
The Commission says the system needs overhauling to take account of free competition and to give callers easy access to the ever-growing number of pan-European services.

The Commission, which will circulate the discussion document to interested parties before making formal proposals, admits the plan will cost money -- rejigging national numbering schemes could cost up to two billion Ecus ($2.56 billion).

But it argues that the price will be small compared with the benefits to consumers and companies faced with different phone numbers in different countries and uncoordinated changes in national numbering schemes.

French telecoms numbering expert Jean-Marc Colomb disagreed. The Commission had underestimated the costs and the technical difficulty of enacting a plan that would change all European numbers, he said.

Colomb, a France Telecom official who heads a working group on numbering for the European telecoms operators' group ETNO, said changes just made in France's numbering system had taken almost 10 years of planning.
"This will be much more complicated," he said, noting that telecoms switches would have to be modified around the world.
The Commission said users must be able to select which phone company they want to use on a case-by-case basis -- by dialing an access code if necessary -- by January 1, 1998.
That is the deadline the EU has set for opening up its telecommunications markets to full competition in most countries.
Common access codes -- similar to the "800" and "900" numbers used in the United States for toll-free and commercial services such as sex lines -- should also be introduced by that date, it said.
By the year 2000, residents of major population centres should be allowed to keep their number when they change phone companies -- a concept known as "portability", it said.
They should also be able by then to select which phone company they want to use on a permanent basis without having to dial an access code, the Commission said.
By 1999, the figure "3" would precede all European country codes, in the same way that "1" gives access to the whole of the United States, freeing the old country codes to be used as regional ones.
That would allow Europeans to contact other EU countries by making a regional, rather than an international call.
British Telecommunications official Larry Stone welcomed the paper's emphasis on fair competition in areas such as "portability" and ensuring that new competitors are allocated numbers fairly.
But Stone, BT's head of EU affairs, said the Commission should be more ambitious and think of numbering in global rather than European terms.

Colomb agreed, saying that introducing the "388" prefix within two years was feasible but he wondered if there was a real demand for it as companies would soon be able to get a toll-free number that could be dialed across the world.
